channel.title: One Author — Data Structures and Algorithms

item.title: Approximating the Girth of an Undirected, Weighted Graph for Larger Approximation Factors
item.description: The girth of a weighted undirected graph is defined as the length of a shortest cycle in the graph. In this paper, we give a randomized $O\left(m^{1+2/(k-1)} n^{1/(k-1)}\right)$ algorithm to approximate the girth of a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges to within a factor of $k$ for any real $k$. We assume that all edge weights are non-negative. For sufficiently high approximation factors, our algorithm outperforms the state of the art by polylogarithmic factors. Specifically, for approximation factors $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ where $c>5$, our algorithm gives a runtime of $O\left(m (\log n)^{5/c}\right)$, while instantiating the previous best $k$-approximation algorithms with $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ yields a running time of $O\left( \frac{cn (\log n)^{2 + 4/(3c)} }{\log \log n} + m\log n\right)$ (Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams, arXiv:2607.00938). Furthermore, the algorithm presented here is conceptually simple, has relatively small constants, eschews single-source shortest path and sparse spanner algorithms, and employs a new technique, which we call ``random filtering.'' That being said, the basic algorithm returns only a numerical estimate for the girth, rather than a witness cycle.

item.title: Deterministic Global Minimum Cut Using $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ Cut Queries
item.description: Finding a global minimum cut in an unweighted graph is a fundamental task in the cut-query model. While there exists a randomized algorithm for this task using $\tilde O(n)$ queries, known deterministic algorithms use $\tilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ queries. We improve upon this result and give a simple deterministic algorithm that finds a global minimum cut using $\tilde O(\min\left\{ nδ,n^2/δ\right\})$ cut queries, which equals $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ in the worst case, where $δ$ is the minimum degree of the graph. The key ingredient in our approach is an efficient maximum $s,t$-flow algorithm, for the case when the minimum $s,t$-cut has value at most $δ$.

item.title: Critical-state algorithms for lot sizing with all-units discounts and variable inventory bounds
item.description: We study deterministic single-item lot sizing with all-units quantity discounts, linear holding costs, and time-varying end-of-period inventory bounds. Unit prices may vary arbitrarily over time. For one common positive discount threshold, we give an exact algorithm requiring $O(n^3)$ arithmetic operations and $O(n^2)$ working space, including recovery of an optimal purchase plan. The method combines a critical-state theorem in cumulative-purchase coordinates with two prefix-minimum scans per dynamic-programming layer. The structural argument accommodates downward price discontinuities and distinguishes prescribed from free terminal inventory. With a fixed global set of $m$ positive threshold values, the bounds become $O_m(n^{m+2})$ time and $O_m(n^{m+1})$ space. Period-specific thresholds admit the same exact construction, but its state set can be exponential. For commensurate flow data, an inventory-lattice implementation takes $O(PW)$ time, where $P$ is the total number of price tiers and $W$ is the largest inventory-lattice width. We also derive a conditional optimality certificate from a monotone one-threshold relaxation; this certificate does not imply a near-linear worst-case algorithm for arbitrary prices. Exact-arithmetic implementations are checked against exhaustive inventory dynamic programs and tier-enumeration linear programs. An illustrative timing study identifies settings in which the lattice implementation is preferable.

item.title: Improved Pass Complexity for Semi-Streaming Matching in General Graphs via Budgeted Price Approach
item.description: We present a simple deterministic semi-streaming algorithm that computes a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum matching in general graphs in $O(1/\varepsilon^{2})$ passes. This matches the pass complexity of the auction algorithm of Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan~[SOSA'21] for bipartite graphs, and answers Open Question~2 of Assadi~[SOSA'24 \& TheoretiCS'25]. Our approach, which we call the \emph{budgeted price approach}, is very different from the previous $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$-pass semi-streaming algorithms for $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of matching in general graphs and improves their pass complexity. All previous approaches are augmenting-path-based and use $O(1/\varepsilon^{19})$ passes by Fischer, Mitrović, and Uitto~[STOC'22], $O(1/\varepsilon^{6})$ passes by Mitrović, Mukherjee, Sankowski, and Sheu~[ICALP'25], and $O(1/\varepsilon^{4})$ passes by Izumi, Kitamura, and Yamaguchi~['25].

item.title: Decoding Failure Biases IBLT Count Measurements: A Gaussian-Selection Law at the Peeling Threshold
item.description: In a self-sizing set-reconciliation protocol, a small first-round Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) sketch attempts peeling decoding; after failure, the protocol estimates the difference count $d$ from the count energy and sizes the second round from a lower quantile of the measurement. This quantile must be computed conditionally on failure: the measurement and peeling success are determined by the same random mapping, so conditioning can shift the measurement law. In the ideal peeling model, inside the critical window where failure has nondegenerate probability, the standardized energy and a statistic of the unsigned mapping that governs the peeling outcome (the precritical score) have a joint Gaussian limit with correlation $η_kρ^2$, $ρ$ being the sign imbalance and $η_k$ a closed-form constant. The measurement conditional on failure is thus a bivariate normal truncated to a half-plane, which we call the Gaussian-selection law. Since $η_k$ changes sign between $k=4$ and $k=5$, under one-sided imbalance the unconditional threshold undercovers exactly when $k\ge5$ and is conservative for $k=3,4$. The key tool is a quenched CLT for a signed quadratic form on a random overlap graph; under asymptotically balanced signs, conditioning on any unsigned mapping event that is permutation-invariant and has probability bounded away from zero leaves the standard normal limit unchanged. After failure the protocol observes the total sign; inverting the selection law yields an upper confidence bound for $d$, asymptotically conservative in the critical window and, when $d/\sqrt M\to\infty$, along the whole load axis. The experiments use analytic constants, none fitted; the unconditional threshold carries a selection error that does not vanish with scale, while the corrected selection-law threshold matches per-configuration empirical quantiles.

item.title: A 0.4584-approximation for DR-submodular maximization over down-closed convex sets
item.description: We obtain a $0.4584$-approximation for nonnegative, non-monotone, $L$-smooth DR-submodular maximization over compact convex down-closed subsets of the unit cube, improving the $4/9\approx0.4444$ ratio of Aggarwal's projection-based algorithm~\cite{aggarwal2026geometry}. A recovery map combining exponential and linear-fractional branches admits a cube-wide affine upper bound. The resulting continuous-time Frank--Wolfe-type algorithm with randomized output and its randomized discrete-time implementation both satisfy $\E F(\widehat x)\ge(0.4584-\varepsilon)\OPT-δLD^2$; the implementation uses polynomially many cube-wide value/full-gradient queries and ordinary linear maximization calls, where $D$ is the feasible diameter and $\varepsilon,δ>0$ are accuracy parameters. Our guarantee and Aggarwal's hardness bound~\cite{aggarwal2026geometry} place the optimal approximation ratio for cube-wide value/full-gradient queries and linear maximization, with additive error $δLD^2$, in $[0.4584,0.4705)$. Standard multilinear sampling and pipage rounding imply an expected $(0.4584-\varepsilon)$-approximation for nonnegative submodular set-function maximization under a matroid constraint \cite[Lemma B.3]{vondrak2013symmetry}.

item.title: Near-Linear Preprocessing for Range Weighted Longest Increasing Subsequence Queries
item.description: We give a deterministic data structure for range weighted longest increasing subsequence (LIS) queries on $n$ values with positive weights. Preprocessing takes $O(n\log^2 n)$ time and space. Value queries take $O(\log n)$ time, and an optimal subsequence of $k$ elements can be reported in $O(k + \log n)$ time. This resolves an open question on truly subquadratic preprocessing with polylogarithmic query time. The key is a single-crossing property of envelopes for value-separated endpoint sets, enabling $O(\log n)$-time persistent merges. The bounds assume constant-time exact addition and comparison of weights.

item.title: Claw-Free and Line Graph Edge Deletion on Block Graphs
item.description: Edge deletion problems ask for the fewest edges whose deletion gives a graph with a specified property. We study two such problems on block graphs. First making the graph claw-free, and second making it a line graph. Since every line graph is claw-free, the second problem is at least as difficult as the first. We show that on block graphs the two optimum values are always equal, and both are attained by the line graph of a forest. The main step is a completion argument, in which starting from any claw-free solution, we put back edges to get some nice structure inside each block still maintaining the claw-free property. This reduces both edge-deletion problems to the same problem of selecting vertices within the blocks of the input graph. We solve it by dynamic programming in $O(n+m)$ time, which also produces an optimal deletion set and a forest whose line graph is what remains after the completion argument. We also extend the method to $K_{1,r+1}$-free edge deletion for every fixed $r$.

item.title: Hypothesis Selection via Weighted Medians
item.description: Given $n$ distributions (hypotheses) $\mathcal H=\{H_1,\ldots,H_n\}$ and samples from an unknown target distribution $P$, proper hypothesis selection seeks a distribution whose total variation distance to $P$ is close to the best achievable within the known distributions. We give an algorithm that, using $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ target samples, running in $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ time, with probability at least $1-δ$, returns $H_{\hat i}$ satisfying $d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_{\hat i})\leq 3\min_{i\in[n]}d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_i)+\varepsilon.$ The algorithm achieves the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. The running time improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic in the state-of-the-art bound $\tilde{O}(n\varepsilon^{-2}δ^{-1})$ of Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal (COLT 2026), thereby answering their Question~2.

item.title: With Leverage, the Gambler is Not the One Who Gets Ruined
item.description: In this note we explore the following simple question: How does the classic \emph{gambler's ruin} phenomenon change if we allow the gambler \emph{financial leverage}? We show that, with a moderate amount of leverage, it is possible for an (idealized) gambler to sustain seemingly improbable profits over a remarkably long time horizon without ever going bankrupt, \emph{even} if the gambler makes only fair bets. With a leverage ratio of $L = 10$ (less than what Lehman Brothers Holdings had from 1995--2008), the probability of multiplying one's money by $1000\times$ without going bankrupt is roughly $50\%$. More generally, given $L$-fold leverage, and given the goal of multiplying one's money by a factor of $r > 1$, the optimal gambling strategy has probability roughly $r^{-1/L}$ of success. The results in this note are designed as part of the course development for the CMU randomized algorithms course.

item.title: Selecting the 7th Smallest of 16 Elements Takes Exactly 28 Comparisons
item.description: Let $V_i(n)$ denote the minimum worst-case number of comparisons needed to find the $i$-th smallest of $n$ distinct elements. We construct algorithms showing $V_7(16)\le28$ and $V_8(16)\le29$, improving the previously reported upper bounds of 30 and 31. Together with known lower bounds, these results establish $V_7(16)=28$ and leave $V_8(16)\in\{28,29\}$. For 17 elements, we establish $V_5(17)=27$ and improve the upper bounds for ranks 6 through 9 to 29, 30, 31, and 31, respectively. Every new upper bound has an explicit decision-graph certificate verified by a static checker developed independently of the search. We also derive a lower bound for selection from a partially ordered state by combining the Fussenegger-Gabow weight with its order-reversed counterpart. All new upper bounds and this lower bound are formally verified in Lean 4. For $V_8(16)$, we show that a lower bound based solely on the total number of decision-tree leaves cannot establish $V_8(16)\ge29$. The algorithms were found using fixed-budget search, information-guided comparison ordering, and proof-number search. Proof-number search was decisive in finding the 28-comparison algorithm; in our experiments, refuting a comparison budget remained substantially more expensive than finding an algorithm within it.

item.title: Optimal Support Size Testing
item.description: We present an optimal tester for support size that determines whether an unknown probability distribution is supported on $n$ elements or $\varepsilon$-far away (in total variation distance) with sample complexity $Θ(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)})$, improving the prior best $O(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)} \log(\min\{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, n\}))$ due to Ferreira Pinto Jr. and Harms (STOC 2025). As a generalization, we provide a pretty good lower bound on support size.

item.title: Semi-Streaming Estimation of the Held--Karp Bound and Graph-Metric TSP Cost
item.description: The Held--Karp bound is a linear-programming lower bound for the metric traveling salesperson problem (TSP). We approximate this bound in the multi-pass insertion-only streaming model for metrics induced by connected positive-weight graphs. For an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge graph and $0<\eps\le1/2$, the algorithm returns a $(1+\eps)$ upper approximation with high probability, using $\wtO(\eps^{-4})$ passes, $\wtO(n\eps^{-2})$ words, and $\wtO(m\eps^{-4})$ arithmetic operations per pass. We replace the changing edge-weight vector by a short history of multiplicative-weights (MWU) updates. After initialization, updates repeat until a column is removed. We store each repeated update once, with its repetition count. The record length depends on the number of columns, not updates; the argument applies to any fixed nonnegative matrix. For Held--Karp, tree-path queries recover edge weights from these records. Separate search and update thresholds allow fresh sparsifiers at successive search stages. Controlled rounding gives a bounded-precision implementation. The estimate yields a $(3/2+\eps)$ graph-metric TSP value estimate and a $(7/5+\eps)$ estimate when the input graph is unweighted. Conversely, in weighted graph streams, every one-pass $(1+η)$ upper approximation to Held--Karp, for fixed $0\leη<1$, requires quadratic space. The algorithms estimate values; they do not construct tours within these bounds.

item.title: A Randomized Approximation Algorithm for Doubly Free-Boundary Macdonald Processes
item.description: We construct an approximate sampler for finite doubly free-boundary Macdonald rail-yard processes with Macdonald, boundary, and edge parameters in $(0,1)$. The construction allows arbitrary finite sequences of additions and removals of horizontal or vertical strips and all four boundary types. It reverses a finite commutation--reflection history from a partition sequence whose entries are equal, with the common partition weighted by both boundaries. We derive local reconstruction kernels from the skew Cauchy, Littlewood, and branching identities. Bulk and boundary updates combine integer increments with conditional shape sampling at a prescribed size; same-sign swaps use finite conditional resampling. For $K$ reflection periods and an initial partition-size cutoff $M$, the algorithm terminates almost surely and samples the resulting approximating law exactly. We prove total variation convergence to the target process as $K,M\to\infty$ and give explicit bounds for both truncation errors, decaying geometrically in the cutoffs for fixed input parameters. Under fixed parameter bounds, we also bound the expected operation count of direct enumeration in a unit-cost model. We further construct an exact rejection sampler for the initial partition law without a size cutoff or evaluation of its normalizing constant. Using this sampler removes the size-truncation error, leaving only the error from the finite reflection history.

item.title: A Deterministic Near-Linear Time Approximation Algorithm for Restricted Shortest Paths in Directed Graphs
item.description: In the restricted shortest paths problem, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge directed graph $G$ whose edges are assigned two non-negative weights (or resources) called lengths and costs, a source vertex $s$, and a cost threshold $C$. The goal is to find, for each target vertex $t$, the length of the shortest $(s,t)$-path whose total cost is at most $C$. Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, and Karczmarz (SODA 2025) gave the first randomized bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm on directed graphs running in sub-$mn$ time, answering a problem posed by Bernstein (SODA 2012). We substantially improve this on two fronts, supplying a deterministic bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time. Our approach straightforwardly generalizes to more than two resources. For $k$ resources, a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon_1,\ldots,1+\varepsilon_k)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time is possible, with $\varepsilon_1=\ldots=\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon$.

item.title: PHastR: Faster Minimal Perfect Hashing with Rotated Layouts
item.description: We present PHastR, a minimal perfect hash function of the PHast family. Like PHast+, the fast-to-build variant of PHast, PHastR finds feasible seeds with bit-parallel operations: its seeds move keys along rings of slots, and to evaluate the seeds of a bucket it cyclically shifts, for each key, a word recording which slots of its ring are used. Unlike PHast+, however, it avoids self-collisions, which make two keys of a bucket collide for (almost) all its seeds: more than a third of the buckets bumped by PHast+ with wrapping and multiplier 3 contain one. With 8-bit seeds, PHastR uses $1.94$ bits per key, the same space as the best variant of PHast+ with wrapping, but it is built in $37\%$ of the time, and its queries are $28\%$ faster on $10^9$ keys, as it bumps $0.5\%$ of the keys instead of $3.9\%$; they are faster also than those of PHast, which takes eleven times as long to build, and about as fast as those of PtrHash, which uses more than one bit per key more. With a larger expected bucket size PHastR comes within $0.02$ bits per key of the space of PHast, using $1.90$ bits per key, and still has faster queries. Its construction also scales better with the number of threads: with all the threads of a 48-core machine it is almost three times faster than that of PHast+. Finally, we argue that when each key can be placed only within a range of $W$ slots, every placement of $n$ random keys on $n$ slots, however found, must bump on large key sets a constant fraction of the keys: we derive a lower bound of about $0.1/W$ on this fraction, and we estimate that the best placement bumps about $1/2W$ of the keys, which is about on tenth of the keys bumped by PHastR.

item.title: Nearly Optimal Quantum Sample Complexity of Learning Fourier-Sparse Boolean Functions
item.description: We study the number of uniform quantum examples needed to exactly learn a Boolean function with at most $k$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. We give a learner with near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(k)$ sample complexity independent of the input length $n$. The learner uses only separate measurements of individual examples. This improves the previous $O(k^{3/2}\log^2 k)$ upper bound (Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Lee, Paraashar, and de Wolf, 2021). The main ingredient is a candidate set formed by symmetric differences of subsets from independent groups of Fourier samples. A multilinear majority polynomial combines unbiased random approximations into an accurate witness whose Fourier support lies in this set. Granularity then forces the set to contain the entire Fourier support, including subsets never directly sampled. For comparison, we derive the tight classical sample complexity $Θ(nk)$ by combining known sparse-recovery and lower-bound results.

item.title: Certifying Capacity and Gaps of the Rank-Dependent Gain-Sharing Framework for Ranking
item.description: The randomized primal-dual framework of Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg (SODA 2013) splits each unit matching gain between endpoint dual variables according to the matched offline rank. The gain-sharing function affects the certificate but not Ranking's decisions. Keeping the splitting rule and expected edgewise feasibility criterion fixed, we define certifying capacity as the strongest uniform guarantee obtainable by functional optimization over a prescribed function class. Its shortfall from Ranking's actual competitiveness is the certifying gap. We study unweighted online bipartite matching under adversarial arrivals on graphs with online degree at most $d$ and on $d$-regular graphs. The optimized protocol is tight on both degree-one classes and in the unrestricted setting, but has a strictly positive gap on both degree-two classes, even over all measurable nonnegative complementary splits. In both degree-two settings, we determine Ranking's exact competitiveness and the exact certifying capacity over nondecreasing gain-sharing functions. For general $d$, we optimize over nondecreasing, right-continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $f(1)=1$, using their probability-measure representation. Both the certifying capacity and actual competitiveness converge to $1-1/e$ in both instance families as $d\to\infty$. The resulting gap is at most $1/(2ed)+O(d^{-2})$ for online degree at most $d$; on $d$-regular graphs, it vanishes but is at least $(1/(2e)-o(1))/d$. These results distinguish function-class restrictions from limitations of the fixed protocol and motivate tighter randomized primal-dual frameworks.

item.title: Thin matrix products up to D <= N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, with 3SUM over abelian groups and a dichotomy for coordinatewise problems
item.description: Alman and Vassilevska Williams (arXiv:2610.06783) gave the first polynomial improvements over the textbook algorithms for 3SUM and APSP: deterministic algorithms with exponents 1.9992 for 3SUM, 2.9983 for Exact Triangle and 2.99942 for APSP. Their algorithm has two steps: a matrix theorem, computing N^2/sqrt(D) prescribed entries of the product of an N x D and a D x N integer matrix in time N^2/D^gamma, gamma > 0, when D <= N^eps, for every eps < 0.1204; and reductions from the three problems to the lopsided sparse triangle problem. We improve both. With Schönhage's five-term partial-product tensor, the matrix theorem holds for every eps < 0.172. The preprint's reductions keep a quarter of the matrix theorem's saving for 3SUM and a half for Exact Triangle and APSP; ours keep all of it, by calling the counting version of the triangle problem adaptively and building composite moduli one prime at a time. Together this gives deterministic 3SUM in n^{1.9945+o(1)}, and Exact Triangle, (min,+)-product and APSP in n^{2.9945+o(1)}. We also improve on the preprint's proof sketch for 3XOR and solve it deterministically in O(n^{1.99451}). Which other problems on three lists does the method make truly subquadratic? It solves 3SUM over F_p^d for every fixed prime p with 3XOR's exponents, and over every finite abelian group of exponent p^2, such as Z_4^d, in O(n^{1.99726}). For coordinatewise problems with a fixed relation P on every coordinate triple, a certified exhaustive computation shows that every Boolean P, and every functional P over three letters, either is the solution set of an equation over Z, F_2 or F_3, and the problem is then truly subquadratic, or has a gadget for Orthogonal Vectors, and the problem is then hard under the Orthogonal Vectors hypothesis. Over four letters, just four functional relations, up to symmetry, satisfy neither condition.

item.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
item.description: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node.js 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node.js 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

item.title: Greedy Region Growing: Improved Approximations for Cutwidth, Pathwidth, Flow-Expander Decomposition, and More
item.description: We give a new rounding technique for spreading-metric linear programs, called Greedy Region Growing, which adapts the classical technique of region growing to min-max graph layout problems and flow-expander decomposition. Using this technique, we obtain state-of-the-art approximation algorithms for several fundamental problems. (1) An $O(\log n)$-approximation for Cutwidth and Pathwidth, improving upon the previous bound of $O(\log n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})))$ due to Bansal, Katzelnick, and Schwartz (FOCS 2024). This matches the $Ω(\log n)$ integrality gap of the standard LP relaxations. (2) An $O(\log n)$-approximation for their directed analogues, Minimum Storage and Minimum Register Sufficiency on directed acyclic graphs, improving the previous bound of $O(\log^{3/2} n)$. (3) A $φ$-flow-expander decomposition that cuts at most an $O(φ\log n\log\log n)$ fraction of the edges. This improves the $O(φ\log n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})))$ bound of Bansal, Jambulapati, and Saranurak (ICALP 2026), and is within an $O(\log\log n)$ factor of the graph-theoretic lower bound. The vertex version of our algorithm also gives an $O(\log n)$-approximation for Treedepth. In particular, our results answer several open problems of Bansal, Katzelnick, and Schwartz (FOCS 2024). Technically, we also solve the conceptual question raised by their work: our technique shows how to adapt Seymour recursion to min-max objectives, and constructs $O(1)$-weak local partitions in spreading metrics.

item.title: Can Rényi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
item.description: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as Rényi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on Rényi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a Rényi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.

item.title: Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle
item.description: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $Ω((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

item.title: Almost Lossless Transfer for Cuttable Distributed Problems
item.description: We study constant-round LOCAL approximation for additive local vertex-subset minimization problems. Given a $k$-uniform $α$-approximation on a hereditary source class closed under disjoint union, Bonamy, Das, Gavoille, Picavet, Suomela, and Wesolek obtained ratio $α(d+1)+1$ on locally nice target classes of asymptotic dimension $d$. We prove two transfers with ratios $α+1+η$ and $α+η$ for every $η>0$. These bounds require the stronger local niceness assumption at a larger scale that depends on $η$. The first algorithm keeps their repair construction and increases the radius used to detect errors. We average over partitions of the graph to bound the retained cost without the factor $d+1$. These partitions are used only in the analysis. The second algorithm tests several deletion widths around the errors. In each component of the repair zone, it chooses a smallest union of retained choices and an exact repair. Averaging over the widths bounds the cost counted twice and yields ratio $α+η$. Both transfers are deterministic and computable, use arbitrary distinct numerical identifiers, and need no knowledge of the graph size. Their outputs also satisfy local uniformity guarantees. For 2-domination on graphs of bounded Euler genus, the same planar source gives ratio $19$ through the earlier transfer and $6+η$ through ours. For minimum dominating set, our transfer gives ratio $7+\varepsilon$ on graphs formed by attaching a clique of arbitrary size at one vertex of a planar graph, using the source algorithm of Amiri and Siebertz. This class satisfies our target assumptions and allows nonempty error sets. Its Euler genus is unbounded, so their guarantee for graphs of bounded Euler genus does not cover the whole class.

item.title: nanoflann: A Header-Only KD-Tree Library for Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search on Compile-Time Product Manifolds
item.description: Nearest-neighbor (NN) search underlies countless robotics algorithms, but many state spaces are not Euclidean: orientations live on $SO(2)$ or $SO(3)$ and poses on $SE(2)$ or $SE(3)$, and a Euclidean KD-tree on their raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors. We present a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree library for exact NN search on user-defined product manifolds declared at compile time: the space is composed from base manifolds ($\mathbb{R}^n$, $SO(2)$, $SO(3)$, $S^n$; products $SE(2)$, $SE(3)$, tori) with a single type alias, and the library synthesizes a metric whose pruning is provably admissible, wrap-aware for circular coordinates and double-cover-aware for unit quaternions. Experiments confirm exactness (recall $1.0$ vs an exhaustive scan under the same product metric), where the Euclidean-on-raw shortcut collapses to recall $\approx 0.5^{m}$ for $m$ rotation blocks, with up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force. We further contribute an incremental, self-balancing single-tree index for points under heavy churn (e.g. sliding-window LiDAR maps) or $SE(3)$ trajectories: bounded memory and faster updates than prior work, with an optional asynchronous tail-latency-bounding mode. The implementation is open source: https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann

item.title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration with an ERM Oracle
item.description: A predictor is multicalibrated with respect to a class of subpopulations (formally, of functions on the inputs, called auditors) if, for every subpopulation in the class and every value the predictor outputs, the average outcome among the members of that subpopulation who receive that value is close to the value itself. For finite classes, about $\varepsilon^{-3}$ samples are necessary and sufficient to learn a predictor with multicalibration error $\varepsilon$, but the algorithms that attain this rate enumerate the class, which is impossible for the large classes of interest. We ask how many samples suffice when the learner accesses the class only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples and polynomially many ERM calls, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the class. Its dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal for all learners. When $d$ is at least about $1/\varepsilon$, every learner that can only access the class through polynomially many ERM calls needs $\tildeΩ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples. Learners with unlimited computation need only $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}+d\varepsilon^{-2})$ samples, so the extra factor $1/\varepsilon$ on the dimension term is the price of oracle efficiency. For swap multicalibration, which allows a different function from the class for each predicted value, $\tildeΘ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples are necessary and sufficient. For estimating the error of a given predictor, the ordinary notion is the harder one: the swap error can be estimated with an ERM oracle, whereas the ordinary error is NP-hard to approximate even for classes with linear-time ERM. Consequently, there are classes for which it is computationally easier to learn a multicalibrated predictor than to compute the multicalibration error of a given predictor.

item.title: Assortment Optimization under the Mallows Model: Independent-Utility Choice Equivalence and Its Algorithmic Implications
item.description: The Mallows model is a well-established construct in preference modeling, describing random rankings through their Kendall-Tau distance from a reference permutation. Its compact parameterization and interpretable treatment of preference uncertainty have made it influential across statistics, machine learning, probability, and revenue management. In the latter domain, recent literature has studied the embedding of Mallows-driven choice into assortment optimization. Early approximation schemes in this context require stylized structural simplifications or restrictive parametric assumptions. In the absence of these levers, a highly involved quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme has subsequently been proposed, leaving wide open the question of whether near-optimal assortments can be computed in true polynomial time. The main contribution of this focused technical paper resides in closing these gaps by uncovering a striking independent-utility structure within Mallows choices, and turning this representation into a polynomial-time approximation scheme. Our central structural characterization explicitly constructs a single collection of mutually independent utilities, reproducing Mallows choice probabilities simultaneously for all offered sets. This exact choice equivalence connects pending Mallows-related challenges to the recent approximation framework of Bowers et al. (FOCS 2025) for assortment optimization under independent random utilities. We make this connection algorithmically feasible through a finite-support reduction that produces distributions of polynomial size while controlling revenue loss uniformly over all assortments. Fused together, these ingredients lead to an $O(n^{\tilde{O}(1/ε^2)})$-time approximation scheme for assortment optimization under the Mallows model, while allowing arbitrary product prices, concentration parameters, and modal rankings.

item.title: Many Scores Force Many Reads: An Optimality Proof for Score of Parentheses
item.description: LeetCode Problem 856, Score of Parentheses, admits a one-pass algorithm using $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary registers. Its correctness follows from a local interpretation: every occurrence of () contributes a power of two determined by its nesting depth. The space bound is immediately optimal in the usual programming-challenge model, but the linear-time bound is less obvious. In particular, a direct adversary that forces an algorithm to inspect every character is difficult to maintain under the promise that the input is balanced. We instead prove a counting lower bound. For every $k$, we construct $2^k$ balanced parenthesis strings of the same length $4k+2$, all having distinct scores. The construction encodes each bit using one of two operations, changing a current score $v$ to either $2v+1$ or $2v+2$. Consequently, any deterministic character-query decision tree computing the score must have depth at least $k$. A two-character padding argument extends the result to every even input length, proving an $Ω(n)$ worst-case time lower bound. The one-pass algorithm is therefore asymptotically optimal in the unit-cost RAM model.

item.title: Deterministic Girth Approximation in Weighted Undirected Graphs
item.description: We give deterministic algorithms for approximating the girth~$g$ of an undirected graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and nonnegative real edge lengths. For every integer $k\geq2$, our algorithm returns a cycle of length at most $\frac{2k}{3}g$ in $O((m+n^{1+2/k})k\log n)$ worst-case time. For every constant~$k$, this matches the stretch and the expected running time of the randomized algorithms of Kadria, Roditty, Sidford, Vassilevska Williams, and Zwick [SODA'23, SICOMP'26] and Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams [ESA'26]. In general, it loses only a factor of $O(\min\{k,\log n\})$ in the term that depends on~$m$. The best previous deterministic trade-off, of Kadria, Roditty, Sidford, Vassilevska Williams, and Zwick [SODA'22], has stretch~$k$ instead of $\frac{2k}{3}$ at the same exponent (for even~$k$) and requires integer edge lengths. In particular, for $k=3$ we obtain a deterministic $2$-approximation in $O((m+n^{5/3})\log n)$ time for real edge lengths, whereas the deterministic algorithm of Ducoffe [SIDMA'21] for real lengths has stretch $2+\varepsilon$. Our main technical idea is that a deterministic construction of the Thorup--Zwick hierarchy used by these algorithms may stop exploring as soon as it finds a cycle: the approximation analysis only needs clusters truncated at half the best cycle certificate found, so balls stopped in this way need not be hit. Together with a degree-weighted selection rule, this bounds the work of each level by its number of edges and stored ball entries. More generally, a ball need not be hit whenever the analysis only uses clusters up to a radius bounded by a certificate that the algorithm has already found.

item.title: Minimizing fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices
item.description: Model minimization is a fundamental problem in formal methods, as smaller models can substantially reduce the complexity of model analysis and reasoning while preserving relevant semantic properties. This work studies the minimization of finite fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices while preserving global or local assertions in fuzzy modal logics, which are either fuzzy propositional dynamic logic or a restriction thereof, optionally enriched with nominals, converse modalities, and/or the universal program constructor. We prove that, whenever the multiplication operator of the underlying residuated lattice is right-continuous, the quotient model induced by the greatest fuzzy auto-bisimulation is a minimal reduction preserving global assertions. If the underlying fuzzy modal logic includes the universal program constructor, this quotient model is also a minimal reduction preserving local assertions and a minimal fuzzy Kripke model bisimilar to the original model. In the case where the universal program constructor is absent and the multiplication operator is additionally strictly monotone with respect to~1, we present the first algorithm for constructing a minimal reduction preserving local assertions; the resulting model is also a minimal bisimilar model.

item.title: Improved classical optimization of fermionic Hamiltonians beyond Gaussian states
item.description: We give a polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm that approximates the largest eigenvalue $λ_{\max}$ of a traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonian $H$ on $n$ modes. The algorithm achieves energy at least $λ_{\max}/O(\sqrt n)$ and outputs either a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse state in the Fock basis. This is achieved through a new upper bound on $λ_{\max}$ in terms of the maximum energy of a Gaussian state and $\sqrt{2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(H^2)}$.

item.title: A Catalytic Algorithm for Transposing Unknown Qutrit Unitaries with Tight Query Bounds
item.description: We construct exact deterministic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary $U\in\mathrm{SU}(3)$ using only forward queries. Three queries prepare a catalyst independently of the input state. Four further queries implement transposition while returning the catalyst unchanged and uncorrelated with the output. Two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries and return the same catalyst. Reusing the catalyst implements $m$ transpositions or inversions with $3+4m$ or $3+8m$ total queries, respectively. More generally, we prove that exact transposition and inversion of an unknown $U\in\mathrm{SU}(d)$, $d\ge2$, require at least $d+1$ and $d^2-1$ processing queries, respectively, in fixed causal order. These processing bounds hold for any program state prepared independently of the input state using finitely many forward queries, even if that state is consumed during processing. Both our catalytic qutrit algorithms attain their respective bounds. Moreover, exact qutrit transposition with four processing queries requires at least three preparation queries, and our construction attains this bound.

item.title: Improved Approximations for Vehicle Routing with Nonuniform Speeds
item.description: We study vehicle routing with vehicles of different speeds on a complete undirected graph whose vertex set consists of a depot and a set of clients, where the distances satisfy the triangle inequality. Each vehicle has a specified speed, and if the total length traveled by a vehicle of speed $s$ is $L$, its completion time is $L/s$. In the heterogeneous traveling salesman problem (HetTSP), each vehicle executes one tour starting and ending at the depot, and the tours collectively visit all clients. The objective is to minimize the maximum completion time among the vehicles. We give a $6$-approximation algorithm for HetTSP, improving the previous $90(1+δ)$-approximation for any fixed $δ>0$. We also consider two versions of the heterogeneous capacitated vehicle routing problem (HetCVRP). Each client has a demand, and the vehicles have identical capacities. A vehicle may execute several tours, each starting and ending at the depot, and reload at the depot between consecutive tours; the total demand delivered on each tour cannot exceed the vehicle capacity. In the split-delivery version of HetCVRP, the demand of a client may be divided among multiple visits, possibly by different vehicles. We give a $\frac92+2\sqrt3<7.965$-approximation algorithm for this problem. In the unsplit-delivery version of HetCVRP, the entire demand of each client must be delivered in a single visit. We give a $\frac{11}{2}+3\sqrt2<9.743$-approximation algorithm, improving the previous $450(1+δ)$-approximation for any fixed $δ>0$.

item.title: A Refined Analysis for Matroid Secretary with Submodular Objectives
item.description: We study the matroid secretary problem with a nonnegative monotone submodular objective. Elements arrive in uniformly random order, and every acceptance decision is immediate and irrevocable. We give an $8.699$-competitive algorithm for arbitrary matroids. The algorithm first rejects a randomly sized initial segment of the arrival sequence as a learning set and runs submodular greedy on all elements in this set. Each later element receives a fixed weight equal to the marginal value it would have when inserted into the stored greedy sequence. On these fixed weights, the algorithm runs a linear-objective matroid secretary subroutine. The algorithm uses $O(nr)$ value queries and $O(n^2)$ independence queries, where $r$ is the matroid rank.

item.title: A QPTAS for Stochastic Scheduling of Bernoulli Jobs
item.description: We study the classical problem of scheduling jobs with random processing times on $m$ identical machines to minimize the expected sum of completion times, for Bernoulli jobs: job $j$ takes time $p_j$ with probability $q_j$ and time $0$ otherwise, and its outcome is revealed when it starts. The benchmark is an optimal adaptive policy. We give a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme for every number of machines. Previously, quasi-polynomial time was known to give an $O(\log N)$-approximation, and approximation schemes were known only for a constant number of distinct sizes. The scheme rests on a simple observation: it suffices to round the times at which machines become free, rather than the times at which jobs start, to a grid whose width is proportional to the job size, and an optimal policy stretched by a factor close to one already respects such grids. We also show that every policy that fixes the order of the jobs in advance loses a factor $Ω(\log N)$, already on two machines, so a constant factor requires adapting the order to the observed outcomes. Further results include a polynomial-time adaptive rule with ratio $\min\{m,1+\sum_j q_j\}$, a simpler approximation scheme for a constant number of sizes, and #P-hardness of computing the optimal expected cost on two machines.

item.title: Tight bounds and output sensitive algorithms for maximal clique enumeration in link streams
item.description: A link stream is a set of interactions between pairs of vertices, each one lasting during some time interval, and a clique of a link stream is a set of vertices together with a time interval during which all of them interact. A clique is maximal if neither its vertex set nor its interval can be enlarged. All known algorithms listing the maximal cliques of a link stream may spend time exponential in the size of a clique for each clique they output. Here, we approach the question under the light of two parameters of the instantaneous graphs of the stream, their maximum degree $Δ$ and their degeneracy $k$. We prove that a link stream with $m$ links has $O(mΔ^2 3^{Δ/3})$ maximal cliques, and that a link stream with $n$ vertices and $|\mathcal{T}|$ distinct end times has $O(n|\mathcal{T}|k^2 3^{k/3})$ maximal cliques. Both bounds are tight up to a factor polynomial in $Δ$ and $k$ respectively, and the second one improves the factor $2^k$ of previous bounds to $3^{k/3}$. Then we present two algorithms. The first one has setup time $O(m\log m)$ and polynomial time delay $\mathrm{poly}(Δ)\log m$. The second one has setup time $O(m\log m+mk^2\log^3 n)$ and polynomial time delay $\mathrm{poly}(k)\log m$. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first algorithms with polynomial time delay for this problem. We also give an online version of the second algorithm, and we show that our results apply to the $Δ$-cliques and $(Δ,γ)$-cliques of temporal graphs.

item.title: Tight Bounds for Equivalence Testing with Non-Adaptive Conditional Samples
item.description: We study distribution testing with access to non-adaptive conditional samples. Specifically, we give tight bounds for equivalence testing, determining whether two unknown distributions are equal to or $\varepsilon$-far from each other in total variation distance. Our algorithm and lower bound show that $\tilde Θ\left(\frac{\log n}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$ queries are necessary and sufficient for this problem. These results demonstrate that the complexity of uniformity, identity, and equivalence testing with non-adaptive conditional samples are all $\tilde Θ(\log n)$.

item.title: $Ω((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ Lower Bounds for Dynamic Graph Problems
item.description: We prove an $Ω((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ unconditional lower bound on the maximum of the query time and update time for dynamic data structures supporting reachability queries in $n$-node directed acyclic graphs under edge insertions. This improves the $\widetildeΩ(\log^{3/2} n)$ lower bound of Larsen and Yu [SICOMP 2025], and matches the strongest lower bound known for any dynamic problem. The same bound holds for incremental undirected shortest paths and subgraph connectivity. To prove it, we bring the recent framework of Ko [FOCS 2026], which gave this bound for Pătraşcu's multiphase problem with Inner Product, to the multiphase problem with Disjointness. Our main technical contribution is to show that verification in Ko's 2.5-round multiphase communication game makes a one-sided corruption bound suffice in place of discrepancy, which Disjointness lacks.

item.title: Deterministic Distance Selection in $O(n^{4/3})$ Time
item.description: Let $P$ be a set of $n$ points in the plane. Given an integer $K$ with $1\le K\le {n\choose 2}$, the distance selection problem asks for the $K$-th smallest distance among all pairwise distances of the points of $P$. The problem has been studied extensively over the past four decades. Recently, Chan and Zheng (2023) gave a randomized algorithm with $O(n^{4/3})$ expected running time, while the best known deterministic algorithm runs in $O(n^{4/3}\log n)$ time. In this paper, we present a deterministic $O(n^{4/3})$-time algorithm for the problem, matching the best known randomized complexity. We also consider the more general bichromatic version of the problem, where two point sets $A$ and $B$ are given, with $m=|A|$ and $n=|B|$, and the goal is to find the $K$-th smallest distance among the $mn$ distances between points of $A$ and points of $B$. For this problem, the best previously known algorithm runs in $O((m\log n+n\log m+m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\log(m+n))$ time. We present a new deterministic algorithm with running time $O(m\log^2 n+n\log^2 m+m^{2/3}n^{2/3})$.

item.title: Rectangular matrix multiplication from shared-leg entropy
item.description: In this note, we extend the analysis underlying a recent matrix-multiplication result by OpenAI to rectangular products and prove that $ω(1,k,1)\le 2$ for $0\le k\le \frac{1}{2}$ and $ω(1,k,1)\le 1+k+\frac{1}{4k}$ for $k\ge \frac{1}{2}$. In particular, $ω(1,\frac{1}{2},1)=2$ and the dual exponent satisfies $α\ge \frac{1}{2}$. We use the shared-leg entropy inequality and polynomial-multiplication degenerations from that work, retaining two-leg symmetry and the orientation of each sector. Logarithmic averaging produces homogeneous auxiliary profiles. Their powered versions have a common asymptotic slope, and bounding their intercepts gives the spectral constraint $b\le 4a(1-a)$. This yields the rectangular curve by tensor-spectrum duality. As an application, Zwick's algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths in directed unweighted graphs runs in $O(n^{2.5})$ time. Combining the rectangular bound with the $(\min,+)$-product improvement of Alman and Vassilevska Williams further gives $O(n^{2.4999})$ running time.

item.title: Settling the Sample Complexity of Rényi Entropy Estimation
item.description: Rényi entropy estimation has been comprehensively investigated by Acharya, Orlitsky, Suresh and Tyagi (SODA 2015; IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 2017) and consequent works, whereas only the sample complexity of Rényi entropy estimation of integer order has been settled. In this paper, we settle the sample complexity of Rényi entropy estimation of noninteger order, thereby completing the complexity picture of Rényi entropy estimation. Specifically, we show that for any noninteger $α> 0$, it is sufficient and necessary to use \[ Θ\!\left(\frac{d^{\max\{1/α,1\}}}{\varepsilon^{1/α}\log(d)} + \frac{d^{|1-1/α|}}{\varepsilon^2}\right) \] samples to estimate the Rényi entropy of order $α$ of an unknown discrete distribution over an alphabet of size $d$ to within additive error $\varepsilon$. For the upper bound, we reduce the bias using a refined polynomial approximation estimator for large probabilities. For the lower bound, we employ a different hard instance equipped with a new moment matching construction. The constructive moment matching has constant bounded high-order moments, while attaining a fixed ratio between the $α$-th moments, which is of independent interest.

item.title: Truly Sub-$3^n$ Min-Sum Subset Convolution and Join Ordering
item.description: We present a deterministic reduction from min-sum subset convolution to min-plus matrix product. We show that if the min-plus product of two $D\times D$ matrices with $β$-bit integer entries can be computed in $D^{3-δ}\operatorname{poly}(β,\log D)$ time for a fixed rational $0<δ<1$, then min-sum subset convolution on an $n$-element universe can be solved in $(2+2^{-δ})^n 2^{O(\sqrt n\log(n+1))}\operatorname{poly}(n,β)$ time. Instantiating this reduction with the recent breakthrough on subcubic min-plus matrix product by Alman and Vassilevska Williams gives a Las Vegas algorithm with expected running time $O^*(2.9987^n)$ and a deterministic algorithm with running time $O^*(2.9997^n)$, strictly breaking the longstanding $3^n$ computational barrier. Notably, these speedups translate directly to database query optimization, yielding the same expected and deterministic running-time bounds for join ordering under the $C_{\mathrm{out}}$ cost function.

item.title: A deterministic algorithm for signing bipartite graphs at the Ramanujan bound
item.description: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Bilu--Linial signing problem on bipartite graphs. For every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most an integer $Δ\ge3$, the algorithm assigns signs to its edges so that the signed adjacency matrix has operator norm strictly less than $2\sqrt{Δ-1}$. Our algorithm builds on the randomized recursive repair framework of Jadbabaie, Saberi, and Sra~\cite{JSS26}, with deterministic rules for sign selection and vertex deletion.

item.title: An $n^{0.3+\varepsilon}$-Approximation for Steiner $k$-Forest
item.description: We give an $n^{0.3+\varepsilon}$-approximation algorithm for the Steiner $k$-Forest problem, for any constant $\varepsilon>0$. As a function of $n$, this improves over the $O(\min\{\sqrt{n},\sqrt{k}\})$-approximation of Gupta et al. [ESA'07, TALG'10] which has stood for nearly two decades for the general case, as well as the later $n^{0.448}$-approximation of Dinitz et. al [APPROX-RANDOM'14, TALG'17] for the uniform weight case. On the other hand, we show that, due to lower bounds on the Densest $k$-Subgraph problem, the $O(\sqrt k)$-approximation for Steiner $k$-Forest likely cannot be improved. Specifically, we show that for any sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, an $O(k^{1/2-\varepsilon})$-approximation for Steiner $k$-Forest would surpass known degree-$n^{Ω(\varepsilon^2)}$ Sum-of-Squares integrality gaps for Densest k-Subgraph and refute the corresponding dense-versus-random conjecture.

item.title: Fine-Grained Hardness of Approximating Dynamic Time Warping
item.description: We prove conditional lower bounds for approximating dynamic time warping (DTW) over the uniform metric on three symbols. Let $N, M$ be the two string lengths and $n, m$ their respective numbers of runs. Under the Gap Block Disjointness (GBD) hypothesis, for every fixed $κ\in (0,1/6)$ and $δ\in (0,1)$, no deterministic algorithm $N^{κδ}$-approximates DTW on two explicit strings of length $N$ in $O(N^{2-δ})$ time. This matches the known tradeoff between approximation and running-time exponents for deterministic algorithms within any fixed factor greater than six in the approximation exponent. For run-length encoded strings, the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis (OVH) rules out any constant-factor approximation in $\widetilde{O}((nm)^{1-δ})$ time for every constant $δ>0$. More generally, for every fixed $η\in (0,1)$, it rules out $(N+M)^{1-η}$-approximation in the same running time. These bounds extend to every fixed metric with at least three points, including absolute distance on $\{0,1,2\}$. Both reductions use long runs to force equal-symbol matches in low-cost alignments. For explicit strings, we combine Boolean gadgets with deterministic gap amplification to obtain a polynomial approximation gap. For run-length encoded strings, an encoding of regular-expression membership gives accepting instances an alignment whose cost does not increase as selected runs grow. Rejecting instances have distance at least the chosen run length, while the number of runs stays fixed.

item.title: Dijkstra Is NOT Greedy: A Global-to-Local Proof of Correctness
item.description: Dijkstra's algorithm is almost universally classified as a canonical greedy algorithm. This paper challenges that conventional interpretation and presents a simple, direct proof of correctness from a different viewpoint. Contrary to the widespread intuition that the algorithm repeatedly makes a local choice and thereby reaches a global optimum, we show that the logical direction can be read in exactly the opposite way: at each iteration, the algorithm identifies a globally shortest path among all paths whose destinations remain unsolved, and the endpoint of that globally shortest path is therefore solved as a ``local'' shortest-path problem. In other words, the local shortest path is obtained as an immediate consequence of a global minimum. Based on this observation, we formulate a Three-Step Exclusion Method that interprets Dijkstra's iteration as deterministic contraction of the global path space. The resulting proof highlights optimal substructure, boundary-state reduction, and dynamic-programming structure, and offers a conceptually simple alternative to the usual greedy explanation.

item.title: A faster matrix multiplication algorithm through structured optimization
item.description: We present a new asymptotic matrix multiplication construction yielding $ω<2.37115924$, and therefore an algorithm that multiplies two $n\times n$ matrices in $O(n^{2.37115924})$ arithmetic operations over the rationals, reals, or complex numbers. The construction improves the bound $2.371177$ of Dupont et al. within the combination-loss framework for the Coppersmith--Winograd tensor. Our approach combines a shared recursive parameter family with a conditioned optimization procedure that addresses two obstacles: weak gradients at low-mass constituents and competing bottlenecks in the retained exponent. A mass- and probability-dependent rescaling supports quasi-Newton optimization in $212\,820$ coordinates, while a six-control correction balances the three extraction roles at each relevant stage. Positive rational entropy-dual factors and an independent ordinary-string verifier turn the resulting construction into an exact certificate. The verified upper-bound expression lies in $[2.3711592385931075066123,\,2.3711592385931075066124]$. The complete witness and an offline verifier using only the Python standard library accompany the paper.

item.title: Explicit tensors beyond the linear flattening barrier
item.description: We construct explicit n x n x n tensors of border rank at least 3n-o(n), improving the previous record of (2 + $\varepsilon$)n due to (Landsberg and Michalek 2025). We also prove that the linear flattening method cannot be used to establish lower bounds on border rank beyond 2n-1. When n is odd, we prove that this bound is achieved by Koszul flattenings. When n is even, a result of (Landsberg 2015) shows that Koszul flattenings can achieve 2n-2, leaving an open gap of size one. Our 2n-1 bound improves the best known 6n-4 linear flattening barrier due to (Garg et al. 2019) and (Buczyński 2026). Combined, these results show that our 3n-o(n) construction, as well as the construction of Landsberg and Michalek, provide explicit examples of tensors with higher border rank than any linear flattening can achieve.

item.title: Almost Tight Bounds for Isomorphism Testing and Basis Construction in Finite Abelian Groups
item.description: We study isomorphism decision and basis construction for finite Abelian groups of known order $n$. We measure complexity by the number of additions performed in the groups and by the total running time. We give a randomized isomorphism decision algorithm that performs $\tilde O(n^{1/4})$ group additions and runs in $\tilde O(n^{1/4})$ time. This improves the $\tilde O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound of Chen and Fu and matches Bshouty $Ω(n^{1/4})$ lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. We also prove that finding a basis with success probability at least $2/3$ requires $Ω(\sqrt n)$ group additions in the worst case. This matches the $\tilde O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound of Chen and Fu up to polylogarithmic factors. These results separate isomorphism decision from basis construction in finite Abelian groups: their optimal worst-case complexities are $\tildeΘ(n^{1/4})$ and $\tildeΘ(\sqrt n)$, respectivel

item.title: A Fast Algorithm for Maltsev Constraints
item.description: The constraint satisfaction problem over a set of relations $Γ$ (CSP($Γ$)) is the computational problem of deciding if a set of constraints admits at least one solution. The classical complexity for finite-domain CSP($Γ$) is settled by the CSP dichotomy theorem: it is tractable if $Γ$ satisfies a non-trivial algebraic invariant and is NP-complete otherwise. However, not all these algebraic invariants result in efficient algorithms despite being theoretically tractable. A notable case that generalizes linear equations is that of Maltsev CSPs: an $n$-variable instance with $m$ constraints is solvable in roughly $O(n^8 \cdot m)$ time by Bulatov and Dalmau (SIAM J. Comput. 2006) or $O(n^4 \cdot m)$ time by Dyer and Richerby (SIAM J. Comput. 2013). At the same time, arguably, most "natural" and efficiently usable polynomial-time algorithms rarely exceed a quadratic or cubic time bound. In this paper we revisit Maltsev constraints with this question in mind and find a $O(n^2 \cdot m)$ algorithm (for finite languages, for infinite languages we in addition need to take the total size of the instance into account). The main novel idea is to not attempt to improve the bottleneck in Bulatov and Dalmau (the Fix-Values procedure) but to avoid it altogether with a slightly more refined approach that allows us to search through a smaller space.

item.title: Efficient Posterior Sampling for $\mathbb Z_2$ Synchronization
item.description: Consider the $\mathbb Z_2$ synchronization problem \[ \boldsymbol{Y} = \fracλ{\sqrt n} θθ^{\top} + \boldsymbol{Z}, \] where $θ$ is uniform on $\{-1,1\}^n$ and $\boldsymbol{Z}$ is an independent Gaussian Wigner matrix with off-diagonal variance one. We give a polynomial-time posterior sampling algorithm for every fixed $λ>1$, for which the conditional output law converges to the posterior in total variation, in expectation over the observation. The construction combines sequential TAP proposals with an independence Metropolis correction. The key is to control signed overlaps after logarithmic pinning and conditional TAP approximations along a random revealing path, which give an efficiently evaluable proposal with a polynomial density-ratio bound outside a set of vanishing posterior mass. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time posterior sampler for $\mathbb Z_2$ synchronization with a total-variation guarantee throughout the supercritical regime. For comparison, the diffusion-based sampler of \cite{montanari2023posterior} gives normalized Wasserstein guarantees at sufficiently large fixed signal-to-noise ratio.

item.title: Almost-Linear Decremental Single-Source Distance Estimates in Directed Graphs via Cut Balance
item.description: We give a deterministic reduction for maintaining simultaneous approximate single-source distance estimates in online decremental directed graphs. For positive integer weights in $[1,W]$, the algorithm maintains an explicit array of integer $(1+\varepsilon)$ upper estimates, identifies unreachable vertices exactly, and answers numerical queries in constant time. Let $N=m+n$, $S=N+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil$, and assume $\log W=\operatorname{polylog}(S)$. Initialization and all updates take $O(Δ)+(N+Δ_{\mathrm{eff}}+\mathcal{L}/\varepsilon)S^{o(1)}$ time, where $Δ$ counts raw updates, $Δ_{\mathrm{eff}}=O(m(1+\log W)/\varepsilon)$ counts filtered updates, and $\mathcal{L}$ measures finite distance growth weighted by the current indegrees of the reachable subgraph. Removed edges and vertices that become unreachable incur no subsequent growth charge. Consequently, the worst-case bound is $O(Δ)+(N/\varepsilon)S^{o(1)}$, which is almost linear for subpolynomial inverse accuracy. The reduction uses the dynamic minimum-ratio cut and exact reachability algorithms of van den Brand et al. (FOCS 2024). A degree-weighted clipped logarithmic potential turns constant relative cut balance into accuracy at every target; a successor cut then restores strict feasibility. A distance warm start and the energy released by decreasing return coefficients yield the refined growth bound. Return mass also amplifies the accuracy of the existing change detector. The public estimates can be monotone, with $O(n+\mathcal{J}/\varepsilon)$ array writes for an unweighted finite-growth measure $\mathcal{J}\le\mathcal{L}$. Execution uses rational arithmetic. A separate reduction extends the worst-case guarantee to nonnegative integer weights. The algorithm maintains numerical estimates and does not provide fast path reporting.

item.title: A Tardos-Type Algorithm for Separable Convex Quadratic Programming
item.description: We give an exact algorithm for continuous separable convex quadratic programming with an integer equality matrix and nonnegative variables. The number of rational arithmetic operations and comparisons is polynomial in the dimensions and the encoding length of the constraint matrix, independently of the right-hand side, linear costs, and all nonnegative quadratic weights. Intermediate rational encodings are polynomial in the complete input. This yields a strongly polynomial algorithm for every integer matrix class with polynomially bounded entry encodings, including arbitrary matrices with entries in $\{0,\pm1\}$. The local solver compresses a quadratic objective on an integer box and solves only the compressed continuous problem. Two-sided proximity on boxes with rational bounds transfers its solution to a nearby original optimum; integer optima are used only in the proof. A single linear program supplies an error bound and a dual potential, while tight-coordinate revelation and fixed feasible anchors ensure termination and control encoding lengths. An explicit lifting extends the result to convex piecewise quadratic functions of signed integer affine features, with operation counts independent of breakpoints and objective coefficients. Applications include continuous multicommodity flow with shared capacities and piecewise quadratic costs of aggregate congestion.

item.title: Approximating Random Walks in $\widetilde{O}(\log n + \log^2 κ)$ Space for $κ$-Conditioned Graphs
item.description: For $κ>1$, a directed graph is $κ$-conditioned if it is $κ$-mixing and its stationary distribution is approximated by the uniform distribution within a factor of $κ$. We present a deterministic algorithm that approximates the stationary distribution of a $κ$-conditioned graph to inverse polynomial relative error in $O((\log n + \log^2 κ) \log \log n)$ space. In the regime $κ= \exp(Θ(\log^αn))$ for any $α\in (0, 2/3)$, our result improves the best-known $O(\log n \sqrt{\log κ} / \sqrt{\log \log n})$ space bound for approximating $κ$-step random walks in general directed graphs by [Hoza, RANDOM 2021]. We release this preliminary version due to recent rumors of LLM-based progress on related problems and uncertainty about when those results may appear. Further implementation details will be provided in a subsequent version.

item.title: Random Order in Quantum Streaming: Replenishment and Robust Lower Bounds
item.description: How can random order change the role of quantum memory in streaming? Later classical input can restore the usefulness of a quantum state consumed by earlier queries. We call this replenishment. We construct an artificial problem based on Hidden Matching, with repeated coordinate data and online matching requests. It admits a one-pass quantum algorithm using polylogarithmic space in uniformly random order, but unconditionally requires polynomial space both classically in random order and quantumly when all updates precede the requests. To prove the quantum lower bound, we strengthen the consumability bounds of Gilboa, Jain, and McClean for Multiple Hidden Matching. Without prior entanglement, any quantum encoding supporting $r$ independent matching requests requires $Ω(r)$ qubits for $r\le N^{1/2-δ}$ and every fixed $δ\in(0,1/2)$, even with simultaneous revelation and arbitrary joint decoding. For sequential requests, the linear bound extends through $r=Θ(\sqrt N)$. We also adapt Kallaugher's triangle-counting algorithm to uniformly random streams in which every edge is repeated equally often. Rebuilding the quantum sketch and resampling the classical estimator improve its expected-space bound in suitable parameter regimes. Finally, we extend the robust Noisy Gap Cycle framework of Assadi and Sundaresan to quantum streaming. A quantum communication lower bound for Block Hidden XOR yields an $Ω(n)$ space lower bound in random edge order for large enough cycles, with consequences for several graph problems. Thus random order can enable replenishment of small quantum representations, while substantial space requirements persist for other tasks.

item.title: Hiding a Vertex from the Temporal Explorer: A Lower Bound for Degree-Bounded Temporal Graphs
item.description: A temporal graph is a sequence of graphs on a common set of $n$ vertices, its snapshots, one for each time step. An agent, knowing the entire sequence in advance, may at each time step wait or move along an edge of the current snapshot, and the temporal graph is explored once the agent has visited every vertex. We consider always-connected temporal graphs, in which every snapshot is connected, and ask how long exploration can be forced to take when the underlying graph, the union of all snapshots, has maximum degree at most~$Δ$. Two lower bounds were known in this setting, $Ω(Δn)$ and $Ω(n\log n)$, realised by different constructions. We establish a stronger lower bound, answering a question of Bastide, Groenland, Michel and Rambaud. Specifically, for every $n$ and $Δ$ with $Δ_0\leΔ\le n-1$ we construct an always-connected temporal graph on $n$ vertices with underlying maximum degree at most~$Δ$ that cannot be explored in fewer than $γ\,Δn\,(1+\log(n/Δ))$ time steps from any start vertex, where $γ>0$ and $Δ_0$ are absolute constants. The construction is deterministic, and every snapshot is a spanning tree with exactly one vertex of degree greater than three. Time is divided into phases. In each phase, a rotating-cycle gadget prevents the agent from reaching more than half of the trees attached to it. Between phases, we reassign target vertices among these trees using walks on a constant-degree expander, and a Gray code order of the targets keeps the underlying degree bounded. The reassignment guarantees that, for any walk of the agent, some target remains unvisited throughout all phases.

item.title: Near-Exact Computation of Independent Chip Model Placement Probabilities for Thousands of Players
item.description: The Independent Chip Model (ICM) converts the chip stacks of the players remaining in a poker tournament into finishing-place probabilities and prize equities. It is the standard model in tournament solvers, but its definition considers all possible finishing orders, and exact computation has been regarded as intractable for large fields. The same mathematics appears in other fields; for instance, the ICM is a Plackett-Luce ranking model with stacks as weights. We present DE-ICM, a deterministic algorithm that computes the placement probabilities of all $n$ players for all paid places in $O(M n^{2})$ time, where the number $M$ of quadrature nodes is fixed for the admissible inputs and the target accuracy. Its numerical scheme allows the target to be set close to the accuracy of double-precision arithmetic. The algorithm evaluates a classical integral representation in which, conditional on a player's exponential clock, the number of players ahead is Poisson-binomial. A double-exponential quadrature on a single grid evaluates every integral; its truncation errors have closed-form bounds, and the step size, which controls the discretization error, follows from the field size. A numerically stable deconvolution then recovers each player's leave-one-out coefficients in $O(n)$ time from one shared product. On exactly solvable instances with up to 4,000 players, the worst observed relative error of an equity is $4.0 \times 10^{-14}$ and the worst absolute error of a placement probability $1.1 \times 10^{-14}$. The full placement matrix for 1,000 players takes 0.2 seconds on one CPU core.

item.title: Prime factorisation of stable-matching instances: uniqueness, simultaneous products, and an exact census
item.description: Every balanced instance of the stable marriage problem with strict complete preferences has a unique finest partition into prime blocks, and that single partition simultaneously factors three different structures: the reachable execution digraph as a Cartesian product, the proposal-prefix antimatroid as a direct sum, and the stable-matching lattice as a direct product. The converse fails, and fails at every size from two on: two explicit families share the identical Boolean-cube execution while one is maximally decomposable with a single stable matching and the other is prime with n. Uniqueness yields an exact census, a recursion counting the prime instances at every size, under which exactly 88,478,208 of the 110,075,314,176 profiles with four agents on each side are decomposable and the decomposable fraction is asymptotically n! / n^(2n). The blocks are characterised as the square components of the mutual-rank filtration, so the partition is computable in polynomial time and the factorisation is a tool rather than only a fact.

item.title: Multilevel Dynamic Thinning for Matroid Secretary
item.description: In the matroid secretary problem, weighted elements arrive in random order, and an online algorithm must irrevocably accept elements forming a high-weight independent set. Dynamic Thinning is a recent, conceptually simple $3.1462$-competitive algorithm for the matroid secretary problem that maintains a random reference set. Given this reference set, the elements in its maximum-weight independent subset have been accepted independently with a time-dependent probability. We extend this approach by replacing the single reference set with a finite hierarchy of nested reference sets. For every fixed $\eps>0$, the resulting algorithm is $(e+\eps)$-probability-competitive for arbitrary matroids, with $O_\eps(n^2)$ queries in the worst case.

item.title: Improved Upper and Lower Bounds for Quantum Convex-Body Volume Estimation
item.description: Estimating the volume of a high-dimensional convex body is a fundamental problem in theoretical computer science. Given a quantum membership oracle for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, we show that estimating $\mathrm{vol}(K)$ to relative error $\varepsilon$ takes $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}+d^{3/2}/\varepsilon)$ queries. This improves the previous quantum upper bound $\widetilde O(d^3+d^{9/4}/\varepsilon)$ of Chakrabarti et al. (ACM TQC 2023) and Cornelissen--Hamoudi (SODA 2023), and achieves a larger quantum speedup over the currently best classical upper bound $\widetilde O(d^{7/2}+d^3/\varepsilon^2)$ of Jia et al. (JACM 2026). Our quantum algorithm combines two new ingredients: an input-dependent effective spectral-gap analysis of quantum walks based on uniform classical warm-start mixing bounds, and a single quantum estimator for products of normalizer ratios in simulated annealing based on classical bridge sampling. We also prove an $Ω(d)$ quantum query lower bound for constant relative error, improving the previous $Ω(\sqrt d)$ lower bound.

item.title: A Potential Function Analysis of Double Coverage for the $k$-Taxi Problem on Trees
item.description: We provide potential function proofs of the competitive ratios of DoubleCoverage for the hard $k$-taxi problem on HSTs and general weighted trees of bounded depth. Buchbinder, Coester, and Naor (2023) obtained these ratios using time-reverse dual fitting and noted that they did not know a pure potential proof beyond $k=2$. We observe that the minimum matching distance between the online and offline taxi configurations can be expressed as an integral over the rooted tree of the absolute difference between their taxi counts below each point. This representation lets us analyse DoubleCoverage over short movement intervals and apply the resulting estimates to potentials that remain unchanged when both serving taxis are relocated from pickup to destination.

item.title: A Factor-5 Conversion to Internal Collage Systems
item.description: A collage system is a grammar-based compression model that extends straight-line programs with repetition and substring truncation. Internal collage systems additionally require every nonterminal to be structurally reachable from the start symbol. Migita, Uehata, and I (CPM 2026) showed that any collage system of size $m$ can be converted into an internal one generating the same string with size at most $9m$, and left the improvement of this constant as an open problem. We show that a simple refinement of their top-down conversion reduces the bound to $5m$.
